pattern.stage: XAT (single computer-based test, Part I + Part II)
pattern.notes: Part I (Decision Making, VALR, QA-DI; 75 questions) and Part II (GK; 20 questions) — reported as 170 + 10 minutes within the 3-hour slot. Part I: +1 / −0.25, plus −0.10 for every unattempted question beyond 8. GK has no negative marking and is not counted in the XAT percentile (XLRI uses it at the final-selection stage). Decision Making comes as caselets of 2–4 questions, VALR has long RC passages and a poem with 3–4 questions each, and QA-DI has DI sets of 3–4 questions; in this mock every such set is served together. The essay section was discontinued from XAT 2024. Options in XAT are usually five; this mock uses four. Section-wise question counts vary slightly by year.

trendAnalysis.summary: XAT has kept a stable 3-hour format since dropping the essay in 2024, with about 75 Part I questions and 20 GK questions. QA-DI has been the toughest section in 2025 and 2026 (lengthy DI sets, algebra and geometry heavy), VALR is dominated by dense philosophical RC passages plus critical reasoning and the occasional poem, and Decision Making mixes ethical/managerial caselets with rule-based analytical sets. GK covers current affairs of the preceding year plus business and static GK and was easy in 2026. Overall difficulty: moderately difficult; time pressure and the penalty for leaving more than 8 questions make accuracy and coverage both important.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from memory-based papers and section-wise analyses of XAT 2024, XAT 2025 and XAT 2026 (held 7 Jan 2024, 5 Jan 2025 and 4 Jan 2026) by IMS, Career Launcher, TIME, Cracku, iQuanta and InsideIIM, located via web search; XLRI does not publish official papers and the full analyses could not be fetched, so recurring question types were consolidated from search snippets and the writer's own knowledge of the papers. Analyses agree on 21 DM, 26 VALR, 28 QA-DI and 20 GK questions, QA-DI as the toughest section (geometry-heavy, lengthy DI) and a poem-based item in VALR. Patterns are paraphrased; no actual question is reproduced. XAT uses five options; this mock keeps four.

passages.title: Caselet: The retested batch
passages.text:
Meera Iyer is the quality-assurance manager at the Nashik plant of Vardhan Pharma, a mid-sized maker of generic medicines. A batch of 4 lakh tablets of an antihypertensive drug, due to be shipped to an African government buyer in five days, failed its dissolution test: the tablets released the drug more slowly than the specification allows. The laboratory retested samples the next day and the batch passed.

Vardhan's standard operating procedure (SOP), approved by the regulator, allows a failed test to be replaced by a retest only if a documented investigation finds an assignable laboratory error — a faulty instrument, a wrong reagent, an analyst's mistake. The investigation so far has found no such error. Completing it would take about ten days.

The plant head, Sunil Batra, has asked Meera to sign the release. He points out that the retest passed comfortably, that the buyer has threatened to cancel the ₹40-crore contract if shipment is late, and that cancellation would mean laying off about 120 contract workers. The release requires Meera's signature; under the SOP, any disagreement about a release is to be referred to the corporate head of quality, Dr. Anand Rao.

passages.title: Caselet: Rasoi Rush
passages.text:
Rasoi Rush is a cloud kitchen in Pune that sells two brands — a biryani brand and a North Indian thali brand — only through food-delivery apps. Its kitchen has six burners and two dum ovens. Between 8 pm and 10 pm, all burners are in continuous use, and the average time from order to delivery has risen over the last three months from 28 to 47 minutes. An analysis by the owner, Kavya, shows that riders typically wait 15–20 minutes at the counter for food; travel time has not changed. The brands' app ratings have fallen from 4.4 to 3.9, and the app now shows them lower in search results.

Between noon and 3 pm the kitchen runs at about 40 per cent of its capacity, and it is almost idle in the afternoon. Most dishes use a small number of base gravies and marinated meats which can be prepared in advance and stored safely for a day.

passages.title: Caselet: Promoted over a peer
passages.text:
Nandini, a software engineer with six years' experience at an IT services firm, was recently made team lead of an eight-member team that builds payment systems for a large European bank. Prakash, who has eleven years' experience and is widely regarded as the team's best architect, had also hoped for the role. Their manager, Ritesh, chose Nandini because the bank had complained about missed deadlines and poor communication, and Nandini had earlier handled a difficult client well.

Since the announcement, Prakash has questioned Nandini's estimates in front of the team, and twice told the bank's engineers in a joint call that a design "still needs his approval". Other team members have begun to take technical questions to Prakash rather than to Nandini. A major release is due in six weeks.

passages.title: Caselet: Clean river, tainted money
passages.text:
Jaldhara is a Kanpur-based NGO that monitors pollution in a stretch of the Ganga and campaigns for cleaner industrial discharge. Its credibility rests on independent water-quality reports, published every quarter, which local media and the state pollution control board often cite.

Shubh Tanners, one of the larger tanneries on the stretch, was fined by the pollution control board last year for discharging untreated effluent. It has now offered Jaldhara ₹1.2 crore over three years from its CSR budget — about 40 per cent of Jaldhara's annual budget — to fund a mobile water-testing laboratory. Without new funding, Jaldhara will have to cut its testing locations from twelve to five.

One of Jaldhara's five board members, Mr. Saxena, is a paid environmental consultant to Shubh Tanners.

passages.title: Caselet: Beanstalk Roasters
passages.text:
Beanstalk Roasters sells 2,000 kg of roasted coffee a month to its retail customers at ₹1,200 per kg. The variable cost of roasting and packing coffee is ₹700 per kg. Its roastery can process at most 2,600 kg a month. Retail demand will not grow in the near future.

The owner, Ashwin, is evaluating two proposals:
(A) A supermarket chain will buy up to 800 kg a month at ₹950 per kg. Supplying it needs a separate packaging line costing ₹50,000 a month, whatever the quantity supplied.
(B) A café run by Beanstalk itself. It would use 300 kg of Beanstalk coffee a month and is expected to bring in revenue of ₹6,00,000 a month; rent, staff and other café costs, excluding the coffee, would be ₹2,40,000 a month.

Coffee supplied to the supermarket or the café costs the same ₹700 per kg to roast and pack.

passages.title: Caselet: Hostel allotment rules
passages.text:
A business school allots rooms to its second-year students according to the following rules:

1. Single rooms are allotted first to students with a documented medical need. The remaining single rooms are allotted in order of first-year CGPA rank.
2. A student found guilty of a disciplinary violation in the first year is not eligible for a single room, except on medical grounds.
3. A student holding a single room must give it up if she or he goes on an exchange term of more than eight weeks. On return, the student is placed in a double room unless a single room is vacant at that time.
4. Married students may apply for family quarters, provided the spouse will live on campus for at least four months of the academic year. Family quarters are allotted in order of the date of application.

This year there are 10 single rooms. Three students have documented medical needs.

passages.title: Caselet: One store, two managers
passages.text:
FreshKart, a grocery chain, is merging its two stores in Indore's Vijay Nagar area into one larger store, which will pilot the chain's new omnichannel model: customers will order online and collect in store or receive home delivery within two hours. The regional head, Rohini, must choose one of the two store managers to run the merged store; the merged store's manager will be judged mainly on the speed and accuracy of online-order fulfilment.

Gauri has managed one store for eight years. It met its sales targets in four of the last five quarters, and staff surveys rate her highly, but she has been slow to adopt the chain's digital tools. Harish has managed the other store for three years. His store missed its sales targets in three of the last five quarters, though it was loss-making when he took over and now breaks even. He led the chain's pilot of app-based inventory management and his store has the region's highest online-order accuracy.

A store-manager position will fall vacant in FreshKart's Bhopal region in two months. Company policy does not allow two managers in one store.

passages.title: Passage: The rise of the meritocracy
passages.text:
When the sociologist Michael Young coined the word "meritocracy" in 1958, he meant it as a warning. His book imagined a Britain in which intelligence plus effort had replaced birth as the basis of social rank, and it ended in revolt. The new elite, Young suggested, would be more secure in its privileges than any aristocracy, because it would believe it deserved them; and those at the bottom, stripped of the consolation that their position was an accident, would be left with the verdict that it was their fault. The irony of Young's later years was to watch his satirical coinage become a term of praise, invoked by politicians who wished to sound both fair and modern.

The case for selecting people by merit is, of course, a strong one. A surgeon should be chosen for skill, not for her family's name, and a society that wastes talent because of caste or class is both unjust and poorer than it need be. Young did not dispute this. His target was not the practice of appointing the competent to tasks that require competence, but the conversion of that practice into a comprehensive theory of desert — the belief that the distribution of rewards across a whole society can be justified by the distribution of merit, and that the successful have therefore earned everything they have.

That belief runs into two difficulties. The first concerns what merit is made of. The capacities that markets and examinations reward — a facility with abstractions, the ability to perform under timed conditions, the confidence to sell oneself — are themselves unevenly distributed by circumstances no one chooses: the books in a childhood home, the stability of a family, the luck of a good teacher. A system that rewards merit faithfully will therefore reproduce many of the inequalities it was meant to dissolve, and do so under a more flattering description. The second difficulty concerns what merit is worth. The value that a market places on a skill depends on what others happen to want and on how scarce the skill happens to be. A gifted programmer is paid many times more than a gifted nurse not because she is more meritorious in any deep sense, but because of the configuration of demand in which she happens to find herself.

None of this means merit should be abandoned as a principle of selection. It means that it cannot bear the moral weight that a meritocratic society asks it to bear. A society may reasonably choose its doctors by examination while declining to believe that the examination has revealed who deserves a good life. The danger Young identified was not competence in office but contempt in society: a winning class persuaded that its success is its own work, and a losing class persuaded of the same. Humility about the role of fortune, on this view, is not a sentimental addition to a fair system. It is what keeps a fair system from becoming a cruel one.

passages.title: Passage: Clock time and task time
passages.text:
Before the factory, the historian E. P. Thompson argued, most working people did not measure their labour by the clock. A fisherman's day was set by the tides, a farmer's by the season and the weather, a weaver's by the length of the piece on the loom. Work was organised around tasks rather than hours: it began when the task required and ended when the task was done. Such "task orientation" could produce bouts of intense labour followed by idleness, and to an observer schooled in industrial discipline it looked irregular and even lazy. To those who lived by it, Thompson suggested, it seemed natural, because the rhythm of work was continuous with the rhythm of life.

The factory changed this not merely by introducing machines but by introducing the purchase of time. An employer who pays for hours, rather than for finished pieces, has an interest in ensuring that each purchased hour is fully used. Hence the bells, the clocking-in, the fines for lateness, the sermons on punctuality and the moral campaigns against the habit of taking "Saint Monday" off. Time ceased to be something one passed and became something one spent, wasted or saved. The new discipline, Thompson argued, had to be taught — and was resisted — for generations before it came to seem second nature.

Later historians complicated the story. Merchants and monasteries had kept close track of time long before the factory; many pre-industrial workers were already paid by the day; and some factory workers retained considerable control over the pace of their work. The neat opposition between task and clock, critics argued, owed something to the romantic contrast between an organic past and a mechanical present. Yet the core of the argument survives these qualifications. What changed with industrial capitalism was not the existence of clocks but the generalisation of a particular relationship to them, in which an hour of a person's life became a commodity that could be bought, and its idle minutes a kind of theft.

The argument has acquired an unexpected relevance. Much contemporary work — in software, design, consulting and the gig economy — is again organised around tasks rather than hours, and many workers are paid for deliverables rather than attendance. To some this signals a liberation from the factory clock. Yet the old discipline has not so much disappeared as moved inside: the worker who is paid by the task, and whose tasks never quite end, must police her own hours, and the line between working time and living time, which the factory drew sharply, becomes blurred again — this time without the continuity of rhythm that once made task orientation feel natural.

passages.title: Poem: The Ferryman
passages.text:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

The Ferryman

He has crossed this river forty years
and never once arrived;
each bank is only where he turns
to take the other side.

The merchants pay him in small coins,
the pilgrims pay in prayer;
he does not ask what they will find
or who will meet them there.

They call the bridge they plan upstream
a gift, a road, a gain;
he coils his rope and reads the sky
and says it looks like rain.

When it is built, he will not cross
to see the farther shore —
the river kept him, and the river
is what he crossed it for.

passages.title: DI set: Orders by channel
passages.text: An online retailer received 12,000 orders in March through three channels. 55% of the orders came through its app, 30% through its website and the rest through partner stores. The average order value was ₹800 for app orders, ₹1,100 for website orders and ₹1,500 for partner-store orders. 10% of app orders, 8% of website orders and 4% of partner-store orders were returned, and every returned order was refunded in full. Net revenue means the value of orders minus refunds. Assume that, within a channel, returned orders have the same average value as other orders.

questions.question: Two cyclists start at the same time from towns P and Q, 90 km apart, riding towards each other at 20 km/h and 25 km/h respectively. Each, on reaching the other town, turns back immediately at the same speed. How far from P do they meet for the second time?
options: 30 km
45 km
72 km
60 km
questions.explanation: By the second meeting they have together covered 3 × 90 = 270 km, taking 270/45 = 6 hours. The cyclist from P has ridden 120 km: 90 km to Q and 30 km back, i.e. 60 km from P.

relevance.note: Second meeting after turnaround at 60 km from P (3D total distance); good XAT TSD with 30/45 traps

questions.question: How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy x² − y² = 45?
questions.explanation: (x − y)(x + y) = 45. Both factors must have the same parity; since 45 is odd, all its factor pairs are odd. Ordered factor pairs (a, b) with ab = 45: (1, 45), (3, 15), (5, 9), (9, 5), (15, 3), (45, 1) and their negatives — 12 pairs, each giving integer x = (a + b)/2, y = (b − a)/2. So 12.

relevance.note: x^2-y^2=45 has 12 integer pairs incl. negatives, with 6 as the positive-only trap; strong XAT integer-solution item

questions.question: A function f satisfies f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every non-zero real x. What is f(2)?

relevance.note: f(x)+2f(1/x)=3x -> f(2)=-1; typical XAT functional equation

questions.question: The sum of an infinite geometric progression is 20, and the sum of the squares of its terms is 100. What is the first term?

relevance.note: Infinite GP sum 20 and squares 100 -> a=8; neat XAT-level progression

questions.question: A straight line passes through the point (2, 3) and cuts the positive x-axis and the positive y-axis. What is the minimum possible area of the triangle it forms with the coordinate axes?
questions.explanation: Line x/a + y/b = 1 with 2/a + 3/b = 1. By AM–GM, 1 = 2/a + 3/b ≥ 2√(6/(ab)), so ab ≥ 24 and the area ab/2 ≥ 12, with equality when 2/a = 3/b = 1/2, i.e. a = 4, b = 6.

relevance.note: Min intercept-triangle area through (2,3) = 12; classic XAT coordinate optimisation

questions.question: A bakery sells 1,000 cakes a week at ₹400 each. The variable cost is ₹250 per cake and fixed costs are ₹90,000 a week. The owner is considering two options: (i) cut the price by 10%, which a survey suggests will raise weekly sales by 20%; or (ii) run an advertising campaign costing ₹20,000 a week, expected to raise sales by 15% at the current price. Which decision maximises weekly profit?
options: Cut the price, since it gives the larger increase in sales.
Cut the price by 10%.
Make no change, since both options reduce profit.
Run the advertising campaign.
questions.explanation: Current profit = 1,000 × 150 − 90,000 = ₹60,000. Price cut: 1,200 × (360 − 250) − 90,000 = ₹42,000. Advertising: 1,150 × 150 − 90,000 − 20,000 = ₹62,500. Advertising is the only option that raises profit.

relevance.note: Price cut gives 42,000 vs ads 62,500 vs current 60,000; XAT numerical DM with sales-volume trap

questions.question: A factory makes two products. Product X earns a profit of ₹40 per unit and needs 2 machine-hours; product Y earns ₹50 per unit and needs 4 machine-hours. 400 machine-hours are available each week, and at most 150 units of X and 100 units of Y can be sold per week. Which weekly production plan maximises profit?
options: 50 units of X and 75 units of Y
150 units of X only
150 units of X and 25 units of Y
100 units of X and 50 units of Y
